title: HyC-LoRA: Memory Efficient LoRA Fine-tuning with Hybrid Activation Compression
problem: LoRA fine-tuning dramatically reduces trainable weight count but the buffered activations needed for backpropagation still dominate memory—69.7% of total in Llama-2-7B—and non-linear operator activations (RMSNorm, RoPE) are the hardest to compress due to outliers.
method: HyC-LoRA introduces two compression tiers. Intra-operator: for RMSNorm activations, calibrate which channels contain extreme outliers, store those at full precision (FP16), quantize the rest to INT2; for attention Q/K, quantize before RoPE application (pre-RoPE quantization) where values are smoother. Inter-operator: LoRA Reorder Computing reorders the quantization and LoRA adapter application so that XA (activation times LoRA A matrix) is retained while the main branch quantizes YW separately, allowing YAB to be recomputed during backward pass rather than stored; Triton-based kernel fusion merges quantization and dequantization with adjacent ops to reduce kernel launch overhead.

title: SMaCk: Efficient Instruction Cache Attacks via Self-Modifying Code Conflicts
problem: Self-modifying code (SMC) detection on x86 processors triggers pipeline flushes and machine clears that are shared between SMT sibling threads, creating measurable timing side channels on the L1 instruction cache that are significantly more distinguishable (150-350 cycle differences) than conventional L1i cache Prime+Probe attacks (1-2 cycle differences). These SMC-based timing channels have not been systematically exploited as a standalone attack primitive for information leakage.
method: The attack exploits the x86 SMC detection mechanism: when an instruction modifies a cache line already loaded in the L1i cache, the processor flushes the entire pipeline and serializes all sibling threads, adding 235-425 cycles of observable delay. The authors reverse engineer which x86 instructions trigger machine clears (clflush, clflushopt, store, lock+inc, prefetch, clwb) using hardware performance counters (MACHINE_CLEARS.SMC, CYCLE_ACTIVITY.STALLS_TOTAL). They construct Prime+iProbe and Flush+iReload covert channels using these instructions as probes on L1i cache sets shared between SMT threads. For attacks, the receiver primes L1i cache sets with nop-filled cache lines, then probes using SMC-creating instructions to detect evictions caused by the victim's instruction execution. Case studies demonstrate RSA key recovery (2048-bit Libgcrypt, 10 traces for 70% recovery), single-trace OpenSSL SRP server key extraction (65-90% bit leakage), and a Spectre-v1 variant (ISpectre) via the instruction cache with up to 4105 B/s throughput. A performance counter-based defense (machine_clears.smc counter) detects attacks with 99.36% accuracy and 0.85% FPR.

title: RTGS: Real-Time 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM via Multi-Level Redundancy Reduction
problem: 3D Gaussian Splatting-based SLAM systems cannot achieve real-time throughput (>=30 FPS) on edge devices; even the most efficient 3DGS-SLAM algorithms run at 0.78–14 FPS on a state-of-the-art edge GPU (NVIDIA ONX). The rendering and backpropagation stages dominate runtime (>80%), with severe workload imbalance across pixels and costly atomic gradient aggregation causing memory conflicts.
method: RTGS is an algorithm-hardware co-design framework targeting 3DGS-SLAM. On the algorithm side: (1) adaptive Gaussian pruning progressively removes low-importance Gaussians by reusing gradients from the backpropagation pass (no added overhead for importance scoring), and (2) dynamic downsampling reduces non-keyframe resolution from 1/16 to 1/4 of full resolution based on temporal distance to nearest keyframe, reusing keyframe identification and alpha-computing results. On the hardware side, a plug-in ASIC integrated alongside edge GPU SMs includes: (1) a Workload Scheduling Unit (WSU) combining pixel-level pairwise scheduling with subtile-level streaming, exploiting inter-iteration workload similarity to reuse scheduling patterns; (2) a Rendering & Backpropagation (R&B) Buffer that stores forward-pass intermediate values (accumulated transmittance T and per-Gaussian color contributions) to eliminate recomputation during backpropagation, reducing alpha gradient latency from 20 to 4 cycles; and (3) a Gradient Merging Unit (GMU) using a Benes network and bypass-extended reduction tree to perform pipelined sparse gradient aggregation, replacing atomic-add operations with structured in-order merging. The design is implemented at 28 nm, 500 MHz, 8.11 W, 28.41 mm2.

title: AIOpsLab: A Holistic Framework to Evaluate AI Agents for Enabling Autonomous Clouds
problem: There is no standardized evaluation framework for AI agents tasked with cloud operations (AIOps), making it impossible to rigorously compare agent capabilities for real-world fault detection, localization, root-cause analysis, and mitigation.
method: AIOpsLab defines an Agent-Cloud Interface (ACI) through which agents interact with a live microservice testbed (DeathStarBench) instrumented with ChaosMesh for fault injection, Prometheus for metrics, and Jaeger for distributed tracing. A 100-problem benchmark spans a 4-level task taxonomy: detect, localize, root-cause-analyze (RCA), and mitigate. Faults are categorized as symptomatic (observable but not causally specified) or functional (specified by root cause). Best-performing agent FLASH achieves 59.32% accuracy.

title: Optimizing LLM Queries in Relational Data Analytics Workloads
problem: LLM batch inference over relational tables is extremely slow and expensive because naive row-order invocation achieves low KV cache prefix hit rates, wasting prefill computation on repeated data patterns.
method: Two algorithms for row and field reordering to maximize KV cache prefix hit count (PHC). PHC is defined as the sum of squared prefix lengths reused from the previous row. (1) OPHR (Optimal Prefix Hit Recursion): recursively splits table by distinct values in each field, selecting the split maximizing total PHC; provably optimal but exponential complexity. (2) GGR (Greedy Group Recursion): greedy approximation selecting the highest-hit-count value/field at each step; uses functional dependencies (primary/foreign keys) to group correlated fields together in prefixes and skip redundant recursion; uses cardinality and average value length statistics for early stopping. GGR runs in under 15s for tables up to 30K rows and 57 fields. Implemented as a PySpark UDF with vLLM as the serving backend.
